documents.title: Follow-up Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Follow-up for BP, cholesterol, smoking, and the diabetes endocrinology is co-managing. Missed the July slot, rescheduled. Says he feels fine, no complaints.

He wanted to spend time on smoking and his health. Which diseases is he actually at risk for? Went through it: heart attack and stroke (stacked on top of diabetes, BP and cholesterol), COPD, and cancers - lung most of all, also bladder, throat, mouth. Lung cancer is the one that scares him; his dad died of it at 60. He has read a lot about how the smoking link was worked out and wanted to talk it through, which we did. He's 49; CT screening for lung cancer starts at 50 and he turns 50 in February - he wants it. Will do a screening visit after his birthday and order the CT.

Still a pack a day. Not ready to quit. Did ask whether the quit pill could be tried again some time - yes, any time.

Meds: metformin 1000 BID, lisinopril 10, atorvastatin 20, olanzapine 10 qhs (psych), ibuprofen prn knee, clobetasol oint prn.
NKDA.

Exam: BP 135/85, HR 78, RR 16. Heart regular, no murmur, no gallop. Lungs clear, no wheeze or crackles.

A/P
- HTN: continue lisinopril.
- Lipids/A1c/BMP/CBC today.
- T2DM: on metformin.
- Tobacco: as above; lung screening in Feb/March.
- Vaccines: flu, PCV20, updated COVID today.

documents.title: Lung Screening Shared Decision Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Video visit, pt at his office on lunch break, identity confirmed.

Turned 50 last week. Current smoker, a pack a day since 15 = 35 pack-years. No cough change, no hemoptysis, no weight loss. Father died of lung cancer at 60.

Shared decision-making done with the decision aid: benefits (finding cancer early), harms (false positives, follow-up scans, rare biopsies, radiation dose), annual scans as long as eligible, and that screening is not a substitute for quitting. He wants to go ahead.

Cessation counseling again; open to revisiting meds later this year.

Plan: LDCT ordered.

reports.study: Low-dose CT chest for lung cancer screening
reports.text:
Indication: annual lung cancer screening. Current smoker, 35 pack-years.
Technique: low-dose noncontrast CT of the chest.
Comparison: none.
Findings: Lungs are clear. No pulmonary nodules. Airways patent. No pleural effusion. Heart size normal. No mediastinal or hilar adenopathy. Visualized upper abdomen unremarkable. No suspicious osseous lesion.
reports.conclusion: Lung-RADS 1: negative. Continue annual screening with low-dose CT in 12 months.

documents.title: CT result

documents.title: Endocrinology follow-up
documents.author: endocrinology
documents.body:
Endocrinology Clinic - visit 10/07/2024 (dictated 10/07/2024)
Re: Eric Strong, 50 y/o man

Dear Doctor,

I saw Mr. Strong back for his diabetes, and he came in with a different story this time. Over several months he has kept gaining weight and feels worn out. His belly has grown and his face has filled out, though nothing about how he eats or exercises has changed. His wife, who came with him, says he's been more irritable lately and noticed purple stretch marks on his stomach. He has no headaches, no change in vision, no nipple discharge.

Medications: metformin 1000 mg BID, lisinopril 10 mg, atorvastatin 20 mg, olanzapine 10 mg at bedtime, ibuprofen 200-400 mg prn knee.
Allergies: NKDA.
Social: pack a day since 15. Weekend drinks.

Exam: BP 156/92. Weight 107.7 kg, BMI 34. Round, plethoric face. Abdomen obese with broad violaceous striae. Proximal weakness in both arms and legs. Point tenderness over the lumbar spine.

A lumbar spine film today shows an L1 compression fracture.

Assessment: the picture is strongly suggestive of hypercortisolism (Cushing syndrome), with a fragility fracture and a rise in BP and glucose. A1c today 7.4%.

Plan:
- Overnight 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test, ACTH, 24-hour urine free cortisol, vitamin D. Instructions given.
- Further imaging depending on results.
- Back: avoid heavy lifting. 
- I'll write again with results.

Sincerely,
Endocrinology

documents.title: Cortisol tests
documents.author: patient
documents.body: The endocrinologist thinks my body might be making too much cortisol and found a fracture in my back. I did the pill test and the urine jug. Should I be worried? My wife is pretty worried.

documents.title: Reply
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Hi Eric - I saw her note. It makes sense to check, because too much cortisol would explain a lot of what you've been dealing with, and it is treatable. Let's wait for the results before worrying; she'll send them to both of us and I'll call you once I've seen them. Meanwhile no heavy lifting with that back. Your appointment here is 10/31.

reports.study: MRI pituitary with and without contrast
reports.text:
Indication: ACTH-dependent hypercortisolism.
Technique: dedicated thin-section sellar imaging, pre- and post-gadolinium, including dynamic post-contrast sequences.
Findings: 10 mm hypoenhancing lesion in the right side of the pituitary gland, measured in the coronal plane on dynamic images. No extension into the cavernous sinus; the cavernous carotids are normal. Optic chiasm clear of the gland and normal in appearance. Infundibulum midline. Sella normal size. Visualized brain unremarkable.
reports.conclusion: 10 mm right-sided pituitary lesion, consistent with adenoma in this clinical setting. No cavernous sinus invasion; optic chiasm clear.

medications.sig: Take 1 tablet (1000 units) by mouth daily

documents.title: Endocrinology results
documents.author: endocrinology
documents.body:
Endocrinology Clinic
Re: Eric Strong

Dear Doctor,

Following up on my letter of 10/07 with results.

- Cortisol after 1 mg overnight dexamethasone: 9.6 ug/dL (normal suppression under 1.8)
- 24-hour urine free cortisol: 286 ug/24 h (reference under 50)
- ACTH: 84 pg/mL (reference 7-63)
- Potassium 3.9. A1c 7.4%.
- 25-hydroxyvitamin D: 21 ng/mL

This confirms ACTH-dependent Cushing syndrome. Pituitary MRI on 10/21 shows a 10 mm right-sided pituitary adenoma without cavernous sinus invasion, chiasm clear. Together: Cushing disease from an ACTH-producing pituitary adenoma.

Plan:
- Referral to pituitary neurosurgery for transsphenoidal resection; their office will call him.
- DXA scan given the L1 fracture - ordered.
- Vitamin D3 1000 units daily, and calcium from food (2-3 dairy servings a day).
- Metformin unchanged for now; glucose should improve once the cortisol is treated.
- I spoke with him by phone today and he understands the plan.

Allergies: NKDA.

Sincerely,
Endocrinology

documents.title: Call with patient
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Called Eric after reading the endocrinology letter. He'd already heard from them. Explained in plain words that a small benign growth in the pituitary is making the hormone that drives his body to overproduce cortisol, and that this explains the weight, the stretch marks, the weakness, the back fracture and the higher sugars and BP. Surgery through the nose is the usual treatment and usually works. He was relieved there's a reason. Keeping his appointment here Thursday.

documents.title: Neurosurgery consultation
documents.author: neurosurgery
documents.body:
Pituitary and Skull Base Neurosurgery, academic medical center
Date of visit: 11/19/2024
Re: Eric Strong, 50M

Referred by endocrinology for Cushing disease. Biochemistry shows ACTH-dependent hypercortisolism, and the MRI shows a 10 mm right-sided pituitary adenoma, no cavernous sinus invasion, chiasm clear. Fatigue, weight gain, proximal weakness, striae; L1 compression fracture. No headache or visual complaints.

PMH: Cushing disease, type 2 diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, schizophrenia (stable on olanzapine), psoriasis, knee osteoarthritis. No prior surgery.
Allergies: NKDA.

Exam: cushingoid habitus. Cranial nerves intact. Visual fields full to confrontation. Proximal weakness at hips and shoulders, distal strength full.

Assessment/plan: good candidate for endoscopic endonasal transsphenoidal resection. Discussed the goals and the risks, including CSF leak, bleeding, infection, low pituitary hormone function afterward, diabetes insipidus, and that he will likely need temporary steroid replacement after a successful operation. He wishes to proceed. Surgery 12/10/2024.

Neurosurgery

documents.title: Discharge summary
documents.author: neurosurgery
documents.body:
Academic medical center - Neurosurgery
Admitted 12/10/2024, discharged 12/13/2024
Patient: Eric Strong, 50M

Diagnosis: Cushing disease, ACTH-producing pituitary adenoma.
Procedure 12/10: endoscopic endonasal transsphenoidal resection of pituitary adenoma. Uncomplicated. No intraoperative CSF leak.

Course: steroids were held after surgery to assess remission. Morning cortisol on 12/12 was 1.2 ug/dL, consistent with surgical remission; hydrocortisone replacement started. Sodium stayed normal and urine output normal throughout - no diabetes insipidus. Glucose managed with home metformin. Walking independently.

Discharge medications: hydrocortisone 10 mg twice daily (NEW; sick-day rules taught - double for fever or vomiting, emergency care for vomiting that won't stop), metformin 1000 mg BID, lisinopril 10 mg qd, atorvastatin 20 mg qd, olanzapine 10 mg qhs, vitamin D3 1000 units daily.
Allergies: NKDA.

Follow-up: endocrinology in 6-8 weeks, neurosurgery in 3 weeks, PCP within a week. No nose blowing, straining or heavy lifting for 4 weeks.
Pathology: ACTH-positive pituitary adenoma.

documents.title: Transitional care call
documents.author: RN
documents.body: Post-discharge call. Home since Friday. Taking hydrocortisone 10 mg morning and early afternoon; knows the sick-day rule. Some nasal stuffiness and crusting, no clear drainage, no fever, no headache. Thirst and urination normal. Eating ok. Med list reconciled with the discharge summary. Appointment with PCP Thursday confirmed.

documents.title: Transitional Care Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
TCM visit, 9 days after transsphenoidal resection of an ACTH-producing pituitary adenoma (12/10). Discharge summary reviewed: AM cortisol 1.2 on POD2, on hydrocortisone 10 BID, no DI.

Feels washed out and achy, which he was warned about as the cortisol comes down. Appetite lower. Nose congested, no clear drip, no headache, vision fine. Not overly thirsty. Back about the same. Still smoking about a pack a day.

Meds reconciled: hydrocortisone 10 BID, metformin 1000 BID, lisinopril 10, atorvastatin 20, olanzapine 10 qhs, vitamin D3, ibuprofen prn knee.

Exam: vitals as charted, weight 105.7 (down 2 kg). Alert, tired. Nares with crusting, no discharge. Visual fields full. Heart regular. Lungs clear. Abdomen striae unchanged.

A/P
- s/p resection, early remission on replacement steroids. Sick-day rules reviewed again; letter for his wallet. Endocrinology follow-up 2/4.
- T2DM: watch for lows as cortisol falls; call if fasting sugars under 80.
- BP on lisinopril, expect it to come down.
- Tobacco: smoking slows healing; offered bupropion again, he declines for now.
- f/u 4-6 weeks.
